Usability testing
Heuristic testing
The Nielsen-Molich heuristics state that a system should:
1. Keep users informed about its status appropriately and promptly
2. Show information in ways users understand from how the real world operates,
and in the users’ language
3. Offer users control and let them undo errors easily
4. Be consistent so users aren’t confused over what different words, icons, mean
5. Prevent errors - a system should either avoid conditions where errors arise or
warn users before they take risky actions (“Are you sure you want to do this?”)
6. Have visible information, instructions, etc. to let users recognise options, actions,
instead of forcing them to rely on memory
7. Be flexible so experienced users find faster ways to attain goals
8. Have no clutter, containing only relevant information for current tasks
9. Provide plain-language help regarding errors and solutions
10. List concise steps in lean, searchable documentation for overcoming problems
8/61

How to conduct heuristic evaluation
1. Know what to test and how - Whether it’s the entire product or one procedure,
clearly define the parameters of what to test and the objective
2. Know your users and have clear definitions of the target audience’s goals, contexts,
User personas can help evaluators see things from the users’ perspectives
3. Select 3 - 5 evaluators, ensuring their expertise in usability and the relevant industry
4. Define the heuristics (around 5 - 10) - This will depend on the nature of the system / 
product / design. Consider adopting / adapting the Nielsen-Molich heuristics and / or
using / defining others
5. Brief evaluators on what to cover in a selection of tasks, suggesting a scale of severity
codes (e.g., critical) to flag issues
6. First walkthrough - Have evaluators use the product freely so they can identify
elements to analyse
7. Second walkthrough - Evaluators scrutinise individual elements according to the
heuristics. They also examine how these fit into the overall design, clearly recording
all issues encountered
8. Debrief evaluators in a session so they can collate results for analysis and suggest fixes
9/61

Usability testing
• Cognitive walkthrough
Examples of questions to ask yourself:
- Will the user do what you would like?
- Will the user try and achieve the right outcome?
- Does the user see that the right action is possible?
- Will the user notice that the correct action is available to them?
- Does the user associate the action with the goal?
- Will the user associate the correct action with the outcome they expect to achieve?
- Does the user realise that s/he can achieve the goal?
- If the correct action is performed; will the user see that progress is being made
towards their intended outcome?

Usability testing
• Thought listing
Potential users (non-experts) perform a task and speak their minds. Analysis 
protocol by expert, identifying issues. Three types of thought listing:
1. Concurrent thought listing
One user at a time, verbalising while using the application
2. Retrospective thought listing
One user at a time, verbalising thoughts after use
3. Constructive interaction
Two users at the same time, conversing about the application
Van den Haak, De Jong & Schellens (2009)
Constructive interaction provides the most natural thinking-aloud as 
test subjects collaborate in pairs to solve tasks
(e.g., a child and an adult)

To ensure that the data collected are relevant and useful:
Define the purpose: Clearly establish what you want to learn from the focus group. This 
will guide the entire process, from participant selection to question design
Choose participants: Recruit a diverse group of people who represent the target audience 
of your research. Typically, a focus group includes 6-10 participants
Develop a discussion guide: Prepare a list of questions or topics to guide the conversation. 
These should be open-ended to encourage discussion and ensure that all key areas of 
interest are covered
Select a moderator: Choose a skilled individual to lead the focus group. The moderator 
should be able to facilitate discussion, encourage participation, and keep the conversation 
on track
Arrange the venue: Set up a comfortable and private space for the focus group to take 
place. The setting should allow participants to freely share their thoughts

Structured interviews
Quantitative research method commonly used in survey research. They involve asking each 
participant the same set of questions in the same order, ensuring consistency and 
comparability of the data collected. This method is particularly useful for statistical analysis and 
is often employed when the researcher seeks to quantify variables and generalise findings from 
a sample to a larger population
Standardisation: Every interview follows the same format, with questions asked in a 
predetermined order and manner. This minimises variability in the data collection process that 
could arise from differences in how questions are presented
Closed-ended questions: The questions are typically closed-ended, offering respondents a set 
of predefined answers to choose from. This facilitates easier analysis since responses are 
standardised
Quantitative data: The structured nature of these interviews makes them well-suited for 
collecting quantitative data, which can be easily coded and analysed statistically
Preparation: Developing a structured interview guide is a crucial step. This guide outlines all 
the questions and the sequence in which they are to be asked, along with specific instructions 
for presenting them
For your further perusal: https://www.scribbr.com/methodology/structured-interview/

Steps in conducting structured interviews
Define research objectives: Clearly identify what you aim to discover through the interviews. 
This will guide the development of your questions
Design the interview guide: Create a structured interview guide that includes all the questions 
and the order in which they will be asked. Ensure questions are clear, concise, and relevant to 
your research objectives
Pilot test: Conduct a pilot test with a small number of participants to ensure questions are 
understood as intended and to refine the interview guide if necessary
Select participants: Choose a sample of participants that represent the population you wish to 
study. Consider using random sampling to minimise bias
Conduct interviews: Carry out the interviews according to the structured interview guide. 
Ensure that the environment is conducive to honest and accurate responses
Analyse data: Code the responses and use statistical methods to analyse the data. Look for 
patterns and relationships that address your research objectives
Report findings: Present your findings in a clear and structured manner, including an 
explanation of your methodology, data analysis, and conclusions drawn from the data

Thematic Analysis
Qualitative research method used to identify, analyse, and report patterns (themes) within 
data. It minimally organises and describes your data set in rich detail. However, it often goes 
further by interpreting various aspects of the research topic (Clarke & Braun, 2022)

cognitions, encounters, or ethical principles of individuals, drawn from a corpus of qualitative 
data sources, such as dialogues, digital social networking personas, or the array of responses 
elicited by questionnaires. Typical Research Questions for Thematic Analysis include:
- In what manner do patients regard the medical practitioners within a hospital environment?
- What are the narratives of youthful females engaging with courtship platforms on the Internet?
- What are the conceptions and beliefs held by laypersons concerning the phenomenon of global climate change?
- In what way is the concept of gender articulated within the pedagogical practices of history education at the secondary 
school level?

Steps in Thematic Analysis
Familiarising yourself with the data: This initial step involves immersing yourself in the 
data by reading through it multiple times and noting down initial ideas
Generating initial codes: Coding involves highlighting significant features of the data that 
are relevant to the research question and organising these into meaningful groups
Searching for themes: After coding, the next step is to collate codes into potential themes, 
gathering all data relevant to each potential theme
Reviewing themes: This involves checking if the themes work in relation to the coded 
extracts and the entire data set. Themes may be refined, split, combined, or discarded
Defining and naming themes: Once the themes are finalised, each theme is clearly defined 
and named. This involves understanding what each theme captures and how it helps in 
understanding the research question
Writing up: The final step involves weaving the analytic narrative with vivid examples. The 
analysis is contextualised within the literature, and the report explains how the themes 
combine to address the research question

Discourse Analysis
Qualitative research method that examines how language is used in texts and contexts to 
convey social and cultural meanings. It goes beyond the literal meaning of words to understand 
the implicit messages, social norms, and power relations that are communicated through 
language (Ho & Limpaecher, 2023)

used to negotiate, perpetuate, and sometimes challenge the social order within various 
contexts of the societal strata and cultural spheres. Typical Research Questions for Discourse

superiority and exclusivity?
- How is the discourse of luxury brand advertising crafted to evoke a sense of modern lifestyle and discerning taste among 
its audience?
- In what manner does the language used in local narratives reflect and reinforce the traditional values and mores of 
crafters and artisans in Sham Shui Po?
- How do social media influencers of high social standing manipulate linguistic and semiotic resources to construct and 
maintain their star status within digital communities?

Grounded Theory Analysis
Systematic method in the social sciences, involving the construction of theories through the 
gathering and analysis of data. It is a data-driven method that operates almost in a reverse 
fashion from predictive research and at its core, it is a general methodology for developing new 
theory that is grounded in data systematically gathered and analysed (Glaser & Strauss, 1967)
Grounded theory is a powerful research method that allows for the development of theory that 
is deeply rooted in the data itself. It is particularly useful in areas where little is known or where 
new insights are sought. The researcher remains open to the data and what emerges from it, 
rather than entering the research with preconceived theories or hypotheses.
Caution: Researchers always have their intuitions and biases, which are unexpressed theories 
and hypotheses!
- It is inductive rather than deductive
- Bottom-up, data-driven pattern detection
- Does not test hypotheses but finds them
Many Machine Learning approaches abide by the same principles

Thematic analysis of Sham Shui Po narratives
The locals interviewed, before anything, emphasise the Cultivation of family values, exemplified by the 
assertions: “family very important,” taking care of family, make family feel good

stylistic devices, such as:
- Onomatope: “ng ng ng”
- Impressionism: air full of dye smell
- (Conventional) metaphors: story telling with hands, stitches stress importance of family, tapestries of life, fingers

nowadays is but a fleeting moment: keep doing what family did, always going on versus cool for a little time
